title: A version-control checkout removes and recreates files with no temporary and no boundary anywhere

provenance.evidence: Five readings. `a.txt` VANISHES at inode 190956880. It reappears at a NEW inode 190956887 with size 0, then the same new inode reaches size 12. Then `c.txt` appears at inode 190956888 size 0 and reaches size 6. No temporary file appears at any reading and no name is ever renamed.
blind_spots: open, flush, fsync and close are invisible to polling

objects.role: a.txt on the branch being left
a.txt on the branch being entered — a different object
c.txt, which exists only on the branch being entered

folder.fidelity: a backend that does not declare ObserveDurableBoundary
folder.omission_note: The zero-length readings of each new file can fall between two readings; the unlink of object 1 cannot, because its replacement has a different identity.

expected.meaningful_durable_change: The whole working tree matches the branch that was entered. There is no smaller meaningful unit: half a checkout is not a state anyone asked for.
expected.forbidden_note: Mount sequence 4 is the trap. It IS a boundary candidate — a.txt was closed — and it is still a half-switched tree, because c.txt does not exist yet. The anchor rule alone does not save this pattern; only quiescence does.

notes: This is the pattern that proves a boundary candidate is not a safe meaningful-save cut. A mid-stream trigger at sequence 4 sees a genuine Closed candidate and still sits inside a half-switched tree. The oracle schedules that trigger and requires the meaningful window to remain open until quiescence at 7.

It is declared NOT safely coalescable in the strong sense: nothing in either stream marks the extent of the operation. A crash inside a checkout leaves a half-switched tree, and the honest response is to record that state rather than to invent the completed one.

There is a real deletion window at sequence 1: a.txt is gone and its replacement has not been created. It is not a save gone wrong — the file genuinely was removed — but a checkpoint there attributes a deletion to the person rather than to the checkout.
